title: No One Architecture Fits All: A Cross-Environment Evaluation of Hierarchical Red Team Agents

paper.title: No One Architecture Fits All: A Cross-Environment Evaluation of Hierarchical Red Team Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract Autonomous red team agents increasingly stress-test AI-enabled cyber defenses by planning strategy and executing multistage attacks. Reinforcement learning (RL) and large language models (LLMs) offer complementary mechanisms for the planning and execution such agents require, and prior work has combined them in hybrid hierarchies. Yet a given architecture is typically developed and evaluated within a single environment, leaving open whether an observed advantage reflects a generally stronger decision mechanism or merely alignment with a particular setting. We address this gap with a controlled cross-environment comparison of two homogeneous hierarchical red team architectures: an RL planner with an RL executor (RL+RL) and an LLM planner with an LLM executor (LLM+LLM). We evaluate both against expert autonomous defenders in CybORG CAGE-4 and in Cyberwheel at two network scales, across 18 configurations under one unified disruption metric. We find a pronounced environment-dependent inversion. RL+RL wins the compact, densely rewarded CAGE-4 (78.5% disruption success versus 18.0% for the strongest LLM configuration) and the 100-host Cyberwheel network (81.0% versus 50.5%), while a pretrained cybersecurity LLM agent wins the larger, escalation-gated 1010-host Cyberwheel network (55.0% versus 0.0% for RL). A kill-chain analysis explains the inversion through architecture-specific bottlenecks that aggregate success rates conceal. In the 1010-host Cyberwheel network, RL discovers and compromises hosts but stalls at privilege escalation, whereas in CAGE-4, LLM agents obtain privileged access but rarely convert it into operational impact. These results indicate that conclusions drawn in a single environment may not generalize, and that hybrid planner-executor designs should be motivated by specific failure modes rather than the assumption that one architecture is universally preferable.

Keywords Autonomous red teams; Cyber operations; Reinforcement learning; Large language models; Hierarchical agents 1 Introduction Autonomous cyber operations are moving beyond fixed scripts toward agents capable of interpreting network state, selecting objectives, and executing multistage actions. Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL), multi-agent learning, and large language models (LLMs) have accelerated this transition [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . These capabilities are particularly valuable for automated red teaming, where autonomous adversaries can systematically stress-test cyber defenses before weaknesses are encountered operationally. Effective red teaming, however, requires more than discovering vulnerable hosts or executing isolated exploits; an agent must maintain strategic direction while progressing through reconnaissance, exploitation, privilege escalation, lateral movement, and operational impact. RL and LLMs offer fundamentally different mechanisms for supporting such behavior. RL agents learn sequential policies through repeated environment interaction and can acquire efficient, specialized tactical behaviors, while hierarchical and multi-agent RL decompose complex cyber operations into coordinated high- and low-level decisions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . LLM agents instead leverage pretrained knowledge and language-based reasoning to interpret observations, formulate plans, and select actions without learning every behavior directly from interaction. Recent work has demonstrated their potential for penetration testing, vulnerability exploitation, and multistage cyber reasoning [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . However, RL learned policies may transfer poorly when operational dynamics differ from training, whereas LLM agents can struggle with long-horizon context, executable action selection, and recovery from failed decisions [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . The complementary strengths of these paradigms have also motivated hybrid approaches that combine LLM-based strategic reasoning with RL-based tactical execution or use LLM guidance within hierarchical RL architectures [ 3 , 7 ] . While such studies show that the two paradigms can complement one another, they leave a more fundamental question unresolved: how do hierarchical systems built around learned policies versus language model reasoning compare across different cyber environments? Existing peer-reviewed studies typically develop and evaluate a particular RL, LLM, or hybrid architecture within a specific environment or task. Hence, limited evidence exists on whether an observed architectural advantage reflects a generally stronger decision mechanism or simply better alignment with a particular environment. This distinction matters because cyber environments can differ substantially in topology, scale, action semantics, privilege requirements, and defensive behavior. Additionally, aggregate measures such as reward or overall attack success can conceal different failure mechanisms. An agent may discover and compromise hosts but fail at privilege escalation, while another may obtain privileged access yet fail to convert it into operational impact. Although recent LLM-agent benchmarks have begun to examine intermediate milestones [ 5 ] , controlled cross-environment comparisons of hierarchical RL-based and LLM-based red agents remain limited. To address this gap, we compare two homogeneous hierarchical red agent architectures: an RL planner coupled with an RL executor (RL+RL) and an LLM planner coupled with an LLM executor (LLM+LLM). We treat these configurations as architectural endpoints to characterize the strengths and failure modes of learned-policy and language-model-based decision making. Both approaches are evaluated against expert autonomous defenders in CybORG CAGE-4 [ 1 ] , as well as on Cyberwheel [ 9 ] networks at mid-scale with 100 hosts and large-scale with 1010 hosts. Across 18 evaluation configurations and 3,600 attack episodes, we assess disruption success, attack chain progression, behavioral efficiency, and planning cost. Our results reveal a pronounced environment-dependent inversion in architectural effectiveness. In CAGE-4, RL+RL reaches a disruption success rate of 78.5%, compared with 18.0% for the strongest LLM configuration. In Cyberwheel, the outcome differs across the two network scales: RL+RL also leads in the 100-host environment (81.0% versus 50.5% for LLM+LLM), whereas the relationship reverses in the 1010-host environment, where LLM+LLM achieves 55.0% and RL+RL achieves 0.0%. Kill-chain analysis further exposes distinct downstream bottlenecks. RL agents in the 1010-host Cyberwheel environment discover and compromise hosts but largely stall at privilege escalation, whereas LLM agents in CAGE-4 frequently obtain privileged access but struggle to convert it into operational impact. These findings show that conclusions drawn from one cyber environment or network size may not generalize to substantially different settings. This work makes four contributions: • Hierarchical cross-paradigm comparison: a controlled comparison of RL+RL and LLM+LLM red agent architectures as distinct end-to-end decision paradigms. • Cross-environment evaluation: evaluation across CAGE-4 and two Cyberwheel scales, revealing that relative architectural effectiveness reverses across settings. • Failure-mode characterization: analysis of attack progression from discovery through privilege escalation and disruption, identifying architecture-specific bottlenecks hidden by aggregate success measures. • Implications for hybrid design: empirical evidence that future LLM-RL hybrids should be motivated by specific planning and execution failure modes rather than an assumption that one architecture is universally preferable. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We first review related work, followed by describing the architectures and environments, then presenting the experimental results and analysis, and finally, concluding with future directions. 2 Background and Related Work Autonomous cyber environments and defenders. Simulation gyms are the standard proving ground for autonomous cyber agents. CybORG models enterprise networks under partial observability [ 8 ] , and its CAGE Challenge 4 (CAGE-4) defines a multi-subnet, multi-agent scenario with coordinated defenders [ 1 ] . The strongest published CAGE-4 defender is a Hierarchical Multi-Agent RL (H-MARL) expert policy [ 2 ] , and graph-based RL agents target the same benchmark [ 10 ] . Cyberwheel is a complementary RL simulation environment for autonomous cyber defense that models configurable networks at substantially larger scale [ 9 ] . Red and blue agents are almost always developed and evaluated within a single environment, so it is rarely possible to tell whether a reported advantage transfers to a structurally different network. Language models for offensive cyber. LLMs have advanced quickly on offensive tasks. PentestGPT decomposes penetration testing into reasoning, generation, and parsing modules [ 4 ] ; benchmarks such as AutoPenBench evaluate generative agents on staged tasks and surface their intermediate milestones [ 5 ] ; and teams of LLM agents can exploit zero-day vulnerabilities [ 6 ] . HackSynth pairs a planner and summarizer for autonomous penetration testing [ 11 ] , and prompted LLM agents can rival RL agents in network security games [ 12 ] . Domain-specialized models such as Foundation-Sec-8B [ 13 ] and DeepHat, formerly WhiteRabbitNeo [ 14 ] , sharpen security reasoning through targeted fine-tuning. Even so, standalone LLMs struggle to sustain long-horizon campaigns under active defense; evaluated as autonomous agents in CAGE-4, all-LLM teams trail learned policies substantially [ 15 ] . Reinforcement learning and hierarchy for cyber. RL learns attack and defense policies directly from interaction, commonly with policy gradient methods such as proximal policy optimization (PPO) [ 16 ] . Multi-agent and hierarchical RL decompose enterprise-scale operations into coordinated high- and low-level decisions, which is effective for CAGE-4 defense [ 1 , 2 ] . Such policies excel at precise tactical execution but are sample-inefficient and transfer poorly when the network or defender differs from training. Hybrid architectures and the gap we address. A growing line of work combines the two paradigms: LLM-guided hierarchical MARL directs a learned hierarchy with a language model [ 3 ] ; LLM-augmented reward and feedback accelerate RL for cyber operations [ 17 ] ; and our prior framework couples a frozen LLM planner with a trainable RL executor, improving multi-stage attacks against the CAGE-4 expert defender [ 7 ] .
